Reasoning surface

Denominators and Rationality Criteria for ∑𝑛≥2(𝑛! −1)−1∑n≥2(n!−1)−1

Erdős #68 49 pp Equations typeset from the exact TeX
PDFOpen the PDF · 49 pp TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis

The record proves liminf (log LN)/(N3/2 log N) ≥2√2/3≥22/3 for L_N=lcm(2!−1,…,N!−1), by comparing a terminal block of denominators with pairwise gcds rather than an external multiplicity theorem. Specialising a Louwsma–Martino valuation, it exhibits primes 139 and 2593 absent from all later reduced denominators. Coefficient constructions give integer forms MS+k; at fixed moment the remainder changes only by an integer. Rationality criteria use factorial digits and the next integer above a scaled partial sum; the digit argument also recovers the irrationality of e. Two exact calculations give q∤299999! and 𝑞 ≥239990 >1012038q≥239990>1012038. These exclusions do not prove irrationality.

This paper owns the complete problem-specific reasoning surface for Erdős #68, including all registered result families and their boundaries.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #68, which remains open.

Organisation.

The first two sections keep two different questions separate: which prime powers survive reduction (§1), and how large a common denominator must be before reduction (§2). The tail comparisons in §4 require information not supplied by either answer. For the finite exclusions, only the carry criterion in §3 and the computations in §6 are needed. The coefficient constructions in §5 are a separate approach; §7 identifies the remaining inequalities, and the appendices give further deductions, unsuccessful approaches, and formal-source links.

Which prime powers survive reduction

Problem 1.1 (Erdős #68). Is 𝑆 =∑𝑛≥2(𝑛! −1)−1S=∑n≥2(n!−1)−1 irrational?

Erdős states the question on p. 102 of his 1988 survey and, in the same passage, records the expectation that ∑𝑛1/(𝑛! +𝑡)∑n1/(n!+t) is irrational, indeed transcendental, for every integer 𝑡t [1]. Here the sum starts sufficiently far out that 𝑛! +𝑡 >0n!+t>0; changing that starting index adds or removes only a rational number. In particular, no term with zero denominator is included. The expectation for all integer shifts is not proved here. Numbering follows Bloom’s Erdős problem catalogue [2].

Put

𝑑𝑛=𝑛!−1,𝐻𝑀=𝑀∑𝑛=21𝑑𝑛,𝐿𝑀=lcm⁡(𝑑2,…,𝑑𝑀),𝐴𝑀=𝑀∑𝑛=2𝐿𝑀𝑑𝑛,dn=n!−1,HM=∑n=2M1dn,LM=lcm⁡(d2,…,dM),AM=∑n=2MLMdn,

so that 𝐻𝑀 =𝐴𝑀/𝐿𝑀HM=AM/LM. Throughout, den⁡(𝑥)den⁡(x) is the positive denominator of a rational number in lowest terms, and 𝑣𝑝(𝑎)vp(a) is the exponent of the prime 𝑝p in a positive integer 𝑎a. The first question is which prime power present in 𝐿𝑀LM remains in den⁡(𝐻𝑀)den⁡(HM). For the largest exponent the answer follows by specialising Louwsma and Martino’s valuation formula for an elementary symmetric sum . Indeed, ∑𝑖1/𝑥𝑖 =(∑𝑖∏𝑗≠𝑖𝑥𝑗)/∏𝑖𝑥𝑖∑i1/xi=(∑i∏j≠ixj)/∏ixi for positive integers 𝑥𝑖xi. Their lemma evaluates the numerator’s valuation; subtracting the product’s valuation gives the reciprocal-sum form. The proof below uses the least common multiple instead of the product.

The need to check cancellation is already visible in 1/3 +1/15 =2/51/3+1/15=2/5: the common denominator contains 33, but the reduced denominator does not. By contrast, 1/9 +1/45 =2/151/9+1/45=2/15 only lowers the exponent of 33 from 22 to 11. The theorem below tests whether the largest exponent is preserved; a failure of that test need not remove the prime completely. The formula is standard, whereas the two factorial-prefix examples below and the later tail comparison concern this particular series.

Theorem 1.2 (maximal prime-power survival). Let 𝑀 ≥2M≥2, let 𝑝p be a prime dividing 𝐿𝑀LM, and put 𝑒 =𝑣𝑝(𝐿𝑀)e=vp(LM). Let 𝐽 ={𝑛 :2 ≤𝑛 ≤𝑀, 𝑣𝑝(𝑑𝑛) =𝑒}J={n:2≤n≤M, vp(dn)=e} and write 𝑑𝑛 =𝑝𝑒𝑢𝑛dn=peun for 𝑛 ∈𝐽n∈J. Then, with inverses in 𝔽𝑝Fp,

𝑣𝑝(den⁡(𝐻𝑀))=𝑒⟺∑𝑛∈𝐽𝑢−1𝑛≠0in 𝔽𝑝.(1)(1)vp(den⁡(HM))=e⟺∑n∈Jun−1≠0in Fp.

Lean: maximal prime power survival.

Proof. Write 𝐿𝑀 =𝑝𝑒𝑊LM=peW with 𝑝 ∤𝑊p∤W. If 𝑣𝑝(𝑑𝑛) <𝑒vp(dn)<e, then 𝑝 ∣𝐿𝑀/𝑑𝑛p∣LM/dn. If 𝑛 ∈𝐽n∈J, then 𝑢𝑛(𝐿𝑀/𝑑𝑛) =𝑊un(LM/dn)=W, so 𝐿𝑀/𝑑𝑛 ≡𝑊𝑢−1𝑛(mod𝑝)LM/dn≡Wun−1(modp). Summing over 2 ≤𝑛 ≤𝑀2≤n≤M gives

𝐴𝑀≡𝐿𝑀𝑝𝑒∑𝑛∈𝐽𝑢−1𝑛(mod𝑝).(2)(2)AM≡LMpe∑n∈Jun−1(modp).

Finally den⁡(𝐻𝑀) =𝐿𝑀/gcd(𝐴𝑀,𝐿𝑀)den⁡(HM)=LM/gcd(AM,LM), whose 𝑝p-valuation is 𝑒e exactly when 𝑝 ∤𝐴𝑀p∤AM. Since 𝑊W is invertible modulo 𝑝p, that is exactly the stated condition. ◻

The complete valuation identity is

𝑣𝑝(den⁡(𝐻𝑀))=max{0,𝑒−𝑣𝑝(𝐴𝑀)}.vp(den⁡(HM))=max{0,e−vp(AM)}.

A zero residue in long68:eq:prime-pole-survival therefore lowers the exponent, whereas complete cancellation requires 𝑣𝑝(𝐴𝑀) ≥𝑒vp(AM)≥e. For 𝑒 >1e>1, reduction modulo 𝑝p alone cannot distinguish partial from complete cancellation. The proof uses no property of factorials beyond the displayed denominators, so it applies to any finite sum of reciprocals of positive integers. For 𝑑𝑛 =𝑛! −1dn=n!−1, the examples below show that complete cancellation can actually occur; the general valuation formula alone does not predict it.

Two complete cancellations.

A unique maximal exponent makes the residue sum a single nonzero term, so the condition holds automatically. With several maximal terms it can fail. The following examples show cancellation in the factorial sequence itself, not just in arbitrary rational sums. Take 𝑀 =𝑝 −1M=p−1. The table lists every index with 𝑝 ∣𝑑𝑛p∣dn, and every one has valuation exactly one.

𝑟1=1,𝑟𝑛≡𝑛𝑟𝑛−1(mod𝑝2),0≤𝑟𝑛<𝑝2,r1=1,rn≡nrn−1(modp2),0≤rn<p2,

run through 𝑛 =𝑝 −1n=p−1. A hit is an index with 𝑟𝑛 ≡1(mod𝑝)rn≡1(modp), its lifted cofactor is (𝑟𝑛 −1)/𝑝(rn−1)/p modulo 𝑝p. Valuation at least two would give 𝑟𝑛 =1rn=1, which occurs for neither prime among the tested indices 2 ≤𝑛 ≤𝑝 −12≤n≤p−1. That enumeration is a finite calculation separate from the theorem.

The recurrence is run modulo 𝑝2p2, not merely modulo 𝑝p: reduction modulo 𝑝p would locate hits but could not establish that their valuations are exactly one. This is why the zero inverse sums prove complete cancellation in these examples.

For each prime 𝑝 ≥3p≥3, the exponent 𝑣𝑝(den⁡(𝐻𝑀))vp(den⁡(HM)) is constant for 𝑀 ≥max(2,𝑝 −2)M≥max(2,p−2). Wilson’s theorem gives (𝑝 −1)! −1 ≡ −2(mod𝑝)(p−1)!−1≡−2(modp), and 𝑛! −1 ≡ −1(mod𝑝)n!−1≡−1(modp) for 𝑛 ≥𝑝n≥p. Hence every summand after index 𝑝 −2p−2 has denominator coprime to 𝑝p. If a reduced fraction 𝑎/𝑏a/b is followed by a summand 1/𝑑1/d with 𝑝 ∤𝑑p∤d, their sum has numerator 𝑎𝑑 +𝑏ad+b over 𝑏𝑑bd. When 𝑝 ∣𝑏p∣b, this numerator is nonzero modulo 𝑝p, so the exponent of 𝑝p in the reduced denominator stays the same. When 𝑝 ∤𝑏p∤b, the new denominator remains coprime to 𝑝p. Consequently, the two cancellations persist in every later partial sum:

139∤den⁡(𝐻𝑀)(𝑀≥137),2593∤den⁡(𝐻𝑀)(𝑀≥2591).139∤den⁡(HM)(M≥137),2593∤den⁡(HM)(M≥2591).

The primes still divide the corresponding common denominators 𝐿𝑀LM. These are assertions about the partial sums; they do not constrain a hypothetical denominator of their real limit 𝑆S without a further approximation estimate.

We next ask where a prime first divides a denominator 𝑑𝑚dm. This means it divides none of 𝑑2,…,𝑑𝑚−1d2,…,dm−1; it may still divide a later denominator, so uniqueness at its first occurrence gives no uniqueness in every larger block.

Proposition 1.3 (cofinal first prime occurrences). For every integer 𝐵 ≥0B≥0 there are a prime 𝑞q and an integer 𝑚 >𝐵m>B with 𝑚 <𝑞m<q, 𝑞 ∣𝑚! −1q∣m!−1 and gcd(𝑞,𝑘! −1) =1gcd(q,k!−1)=1 for every 𝑘k with 2 ≤𝑘 <𝑚2≤k<m.

Lean: cofinal first prime occurrences.

Proof. Choose a prime 𝑞 ≥𝐵! +5q≥B!+5. Wilson’s theorem gives (𝑞 −2)! ≡1(mod𝑞)(q−2)!≡1(modq), so there is a least index 𝑚 ≥2m≥2 with 𝑞 ∣𝑚! −1q∣m!−1, and 𝑚 ≤𝑞 −2m≤q−2. If 𝑚 ≤𝐵m≤B, then 𝑞 ≤𝑚! −1 ≤𝐵! −1q≤m!−1≤B!−1, contradicting the choice of 𝑞q. Hence 𝑚 >𝐵m>B, and minimality gives the coprimality assertions. ◻

The construction proves cofinality of first occurrences, but not the inequality involving 𝑞q needed for the additional two-factor test in §4. The sufficient tail inequality there does not require choosing a prime 𝑞q. Wilson reflection limits what can be inferred from a large prime factor alone: for odd 2 ≤𝑛 <𝑞2≤n<q with 𝑞 ∣𝑛! −1q∣n!−1, the identity (𝑞 −1 −𝑛)! 𝑛! ≡( −1)𝑛+1(mod𝑞)(q−1−n)!n!≡(−1)n+1(modq) gives the reflected congruence at 𝑞 −𝑛 −1q−n−1. It gives a second summand denominator only when 𝑞 ≠2𝑛 +1q≠2n+1 and 𝑛 ≤𝑞 −3n≤q−3. At the Wilson endpoint 𝑛 =𝑞 −2n=q−2, it instead returns index 11, where 1! −1 =01!−1=0 is not a denominator of this series. The reflection identity is classical; see Stewart .

Status. The problem treated here is open, and this note does not close it. Every statement below marked as checked is a proposition that the pinned Lean kernel accepts from the sources this note links to, with no sorry, no added axiom, and no unchecked evaluation. That is a claim about the formal statement, not about its mathematical interest, its novelty, or the original problem. The unresolved obligations are named exactly, in their own section, and none of the finite computations, reductions, or no-go results here removes one of them.

Companion system context. The claim and trust boundary, cold-clone route to proof authority, and public contribution protocol are described in sibling papers. Those descriptions do not change the mathematical status of this note.

The growth of the common denominator

Theorem 1.2 concerns the denominator after reduction. The common denominator before reduction admits an unconditional lower bound of its own, by an elementary argument.

Lemma 2.1 (product, least common multiple, pairwise gcd). For positive integers 𝑥1,…,𝑥𝑘x1,…,xk,

𝑘∏𝑖=1𝑥𝑖 | | | lcm⁡(𝑥1,…,𝑥𝑘)∏𝑖<𝑗gcd(𝑥𝑖,𝑥𝑗).∏i=1kxi | lcm⁡(x1,…,xk)∏i<jgcd(xi,xj).

Lean: product lcm pairwise gcd.

Proof. Fix a prime 𝑟r and relabel so that 𝑎1 ≤⋯ ≤𝑎𝑘a1≤⋯≤ak, where 𝑎𝑖 =𝑣𝑟(𝑥𝑖)ai=vr(xi). The right-hand side has 𝑟r-valuation 𝑎𝑘 +∑𝑖<𝑗min(𝑎𝑖,𝑎𝑗) =𝑎𝑘 +∑𝑘−1𝑖=1(𝑘 −𝑖)𝑎𝑖ak+∑i<jmin(ai,aj)=ak+∑i=1k−1(k−i)ai, and the left-hand side has ∑𝑘𝑖=1𝑎𝑖∑i=1kai. The difference is ∑𝑘−1𝑖=1(𝑘 −𝑖 −1)𝑎𝑖∑i=1k−1(k−i−1)ai, which is nonnegative. ◻

The next divisibility is the case 𝑃 = −1P=−1 of the relation gcd(𝑖! +𝑃(𝑖),𝑗! +𝑃(𝑗)) ∣(𝑗!/𝑖!)𝑃(𝑖) −𝑃(𝑗)gcd(i!+P(i),j!+P(j))∣(j!/i!)P(i)−P(j) for 𝑃 ∈ℤ[𝑋]P∈Z[X], obtained by multiplying 𝑖! +𝑃(𝑖)i!+P(i) by 𝑗!/𝑖!j!/i! and subtracting 𝑗! +𝑃(𝑗)j!+P(j). Luca and Shparlinski use this relation to bound a common divisor of 𝑛! +𝑃(𝑛)n!+P(n) and (𝑛 +ℎ)! +𝑃(𝑛 +ℎ)(n+h)!+P(n+h) in the proof of their Lemma 5 [13], and Lai uses it for a common prime-power divisor [14].

The earlier spacing method of Erdős and Stewart is related background. We now state only the subtraction needed for the lcm argument, rather than importing the prime-factor estimates of those papers.

Lemma 2.2 (factorial-gap gcd). For 2 ≤𝑖 <𝑗2≤i<j, the integer 𝑔 =gcd(𝑖! −1,𝑗! −1)g=gcd(i!−1,j!−1) divides 𝑗!/𝑖! −1j!/i!−1, and 𝑔 ≤𝑗!/𝑖! −1 <𝑗𝑗−𝑖g≤j!/i!−1<jj−i.

Lean: factorial gap gcd exact.

Proof. Both 𝑖!i! and 𝑗!j! are congruent to 11 modulo 𝑔g. The quotient 𝑗!/𝑖! =(𝑖 +1)(𝑖 +2)⋯𝑗j!/i!=(i+1)(i+2)⋯j is an integer, and 𝑗! =𝑖! ⋅(𝑗!/𝑖!)j!=i!⋅(j!/i!), so 𝑗!/𝑖! ≡1(mod𝑔)j!/i!≡1(modg). Since 𝑗!/𝑖! ≥𝑖 +1 >1j!/i!≥i+1>1, the positive integer 𝑗!/𝑖! −1j!/i!−1 is a multiple of 𝑔g, whence 𝑔 ≤𝑗!/𝑖! −1g≤j!/i!−1. Finally 𝑗!/𝑖!j!/i! is a product of 𝑗 −𝑖j−i integers each at most 𝑗j. ◻

𝑁∑𝑛=𝑁−𝑘+1log⁡(𝑛!−1) ≤ log⁡𝐿𝑁+(𝑘+13)log⁡𝑁.(3)(3)∑n=N−k+1Nlog⁡(n!−1) ≤ log⁡LN+(k+13)log⁡N.

∑𝑖<𝑗(𝑗−𝑖)=𝑘−1∑𝑑=1𝑑(𝑘−𝑑)=(𝑘+13).∑i<j(j−i)=∑d=1k−1d(k−d)=(k+13).

Taking logarithms of the resulting divisibility gives (3). ◻

Theorem 2.4 (common-denominator growth).

lim inf𝑁→∞log⁡𝐿𝑁𝑁3/2log⁡𝑁 ≥ 2√23.lim infN→∞log⁡LNN3/2log⁡N ≥ 223.

The displayed proof of the lcm bound uses only Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2. Its formal counterpart is listed in the sources section; the status of that entry is not a blanket assertion about all linked modules. Theorem 12 of Garaev, Luca and Shparlinski [7] supplies a different input: a uniform 𝑂(𝑁2/3)O(N2/3) bound for the number of solutions of 𝑛! ≡𝑎(mod𝑝)n!≡a(modp), for fixed 𝑎 ≢0(mod𝑝)a≢0(modp), in an interval of length 𝑁N contained in 1 ≤𝑛 <𝑝1≤n<p. The weaker lcm deduction from it is retained in §B.3, not used here. No exhaustive priority claim is made for the lcm estimate; its precise elementary derivation and the inherited subtraction are stated so that the claim can be assessed without relying on a search conclusion.

A non-polynomial comparison.

For linear forms in 𝑝p-adic zeta values, with 𝑝 ≥5p≥5 a fixed prime and 𝑛n the index of the form, Lai, Lupu and Sprang quantify a saving of this kind. They bound the denominators of the coefficients by powers of lcm⁡(1,…,𝑛)lcm⁡(1,…,n), show that the bound may be divided by a product Φ𝑛Φn of prime powers, and compute the growth rate of Φ𝑛Φn [15]. That saving enters the inequality [15] under which the rescaled forms, which have integer coefficients, meet the irrationality criterion [15] that they quote from Lai . Along one unbounded subsequence, the forms must be nonzero and their 𝑝p-adic absolute values, multiplied by the largest ordinary absolute value of an integer coefficient, must tend to zero. The coefficient bound is archimedean; the bound on the value is 𝑝p-adic. The conclusion is that at least one of the finitely many 𝑝p-adic numbers in the forms is irrational, not that each is irrational. The corresponding saving for 𝐻𝑁HN is the ratio 𝐿𝑁/𝑄𝑁LN/QN.

This ratio is an integer. Merely naming it supplies neither its growth nor a small linear form; the analogy is about what an eventual estimate would have to accomplish. Theorem 1.2 decides, for each prime 𝑝 ∣𝐿𝑁p∣LN, whether 𝑝p divides this ratio; no asymptotic lower bound for the ratio is established here. This paragraph compares the two methods; no 𝑝p-adic theorem is applied to 𝑆S.

The basis formula long68:eq:low-channel-basis describes all solutions of the weighted-sum equations, and long68:eq:low-channel-support imposes the support restriction. The remainder identity then determines their residues modulo ℤZ. In particular, R(𝑐)R(c) is an integer linear form in 11 and 𝑆S, and its distance from the nearest integer equals that of 𝑀(𝑐)𝑆M(c)S. Integer translation can choose a representative near zero, but cannot change this distance. To exclude every rational denominator this way, each positive integer 𝑞q must divide the moment of some nonintegral remainder in the family. Eventual divisibility by every fixed 𝑞q is sufficient; growth of the moments alone is not. For example, the compulsory factor 12𝐿𝐷12LD has 33-adic valuation exactly 11 for every 𝐷D, so this necessary divisor alone never guarantees that 99 divides the moment.

Indeed, for a nonintegral remainder the gap is eventually at least ⌊R(𝑐)⌋ +1 −R(𝑐) >0⌊R(c)⌋+1−R(c)>0, whereas the upper bound tends to zero. For an integral remainder, the eventual gap equals the omitted tail itself and is smaller than that upper bound. At any one cutoff, success places the remainder strictly above the finite part and below the least integer strictly exceeding it, so it implies nonintegrality. The short note writes out the inequality in its section “The remaining real comparison”; increasing the cutoff alone does not prove that it succeeds. This is a truncation choice, distinct from prescribing the largest nonzero coefficient index.

The remaining arithmetic inputs

The exact target is 𝑚 ∤𝑍𝑚m∤Zm at arbitrarily large indices, as in (8); the equivalent comparison with fractional parts is (10). The estimates discussed below would suffice for this target but are not proved here. The finite test long68:eq:finite-escape implies escape at each index; its occurrence at arbitrarily large integer indices is also equivalent to irrationality, as proved in §3. Thus the missing step is to prove that this actual rational sequence meets the test at arbitrarily large indices, not to supply another equivalence. Restricting to a prime subsequence or replacing a numerator by a residue imposes additional conditions. A model obeying only selected congruences is not the actual sequence.

Value sets do not determine the weighted residue sum.

Garaev, Luca and Shparlinski’s harmonic-sum estimate concerns unconditioned harmonic sums, not sums restricted to the indices where 𝑛! ≡1(mod𝑞)n!≡1(modq). The value-set literature addresses different invariants. Banks, Luca, Shparlinski and Stichtenoth [25] provide historical missing-value context; Klurman and Munsch [26] distinguish unconditional averages from GRH-dependent improvements. Grebennikov, Sagdeev, Semchankau and Vasilevskii [27] study sizes of value and quotient sets, as do the factorial-residue and representation results of Hu [22] and Garaev and Pardo [23]. None is a noncancellation theorem for the reciprocal unit weights here. A lower bound for the number of distinct residues does give an upper bound on the multiplicity of residue 11, since every other value needs at least one index. But that bound does not determine the reciprocal unit weights or test whether they cancel modulo 𝑞q. The two explicit cancellations in §1 illustrate why the weights matter. Hu’s September preprint [24] considers pairwise distinct maps 𝑇𝜃(𝑥) =𝑏𝜃 +𝑐𝜃/𝑥Tθ(x)=bθ+cθ/x over 𝔽𝑝Fp, with 𝑐𝜃 ≠0cθ≠0. An internal transition is a pair (𝑥,𝜃)(x,θ) for which 𝑥 ∈𝐴 ∖{0}x∈A∖{0} and 𝑇𝜃(𝑥) ∈𝐴Tθ(x)∈A. With at least 𝑀M distinct such pairs, at most |𝐴||A| parameters, and a bound 𝜇 ≥1μ≥1 on the number of ordered parameter pairs representing each nonidentity map 𝑇𝜂𝑇−1𝜃TηTθ−1, the theorem gives |𝐴| ≫min{𝑀,𝑝}8/15𝜇−4/15|A|≫min{M,p}8/15μ−4/15. Its incidence estimate comes from Stevens and de Zeeuw . To apply this to the residue classes of indices satisfying 𝑛! ≡1(mod𝑞)n!≡1(modq), one would first have to specify the set 𝐴A and the transition maps. The number of such indices is not automatically a lower bound for 𝑀M: different indices may produce the same pair (𝑥,𝜃)(x,θ), and their factorial values are all 11. One must prove that enough distinct transitions remain, as well as bound the ordered-pair multiplicity 𝜇μ. The unconditioned value-set theorem does not provide these additional facts.

The shared denominator and the gap must be controlled together.

Stewart’s gap-product estimate [8] requires the two products to be unequal. He supplies that step separately: in the proof of his bound (14), a prime-distribution argument separates the products when the common divisor is large; the smaller-divisor case is immediate .

The non-power theorem gives a different argument when the gaps are adjacent. For integers 2 ≤𝑖 <𝑗 <𝑘2≤i<j<k, equality 𝑗!/𝑖! =𝑘!/𝑗!j!/i!=k!/j! would make 𝑘!/𝑖!k!/i! a square, contrary to that theorem [31]. Selecting two short gaps with nearly equal lengths need not preserve adjacency, so this observation alone cannot replace Stewart’s nonvanishing argument. The wider equal-product problem has a separate history [29]; the doubled-length theorem discussed by Nguyen Xuan Tho [30] is another special case, not arbitrary near-equal-length nonvanishing. No stronger lcm exponent is inferred from these local observations.

Criteria from the literature that do not apply.

Duverney’s Theorem 3.1 assumes, among other conditions, quadratic growth 𝑐𝑢2𝑛 ≤𝑢𝑛+1 ≤𝑐′𝑢2𝑛cun2≤un+1≤c′un2 for positive constants 𝑐,𝑐′c,c′. For 𝑢𝑛 =𝑛! −1un=n!−1, however, 𝑢𝑛+1/𝑢2𝑛 →0un+1/un2→0. His Corollary 3.2 assumes convergence of the signed series ∑𝑛(𝑢𝑛+1/𝑢2𝑛 −1)∑n(un+1/un2−1) in (3.6). Here its terms tend to −1−1, so that hypothesis fails as well [10]. For a single denominator sequence the rapid-growth criterion goes back to Erdős [3]; Barreto, Kang, Kim, Kovač and Zhang treat products of consecutive denominators and weighted extensions . For 𝑎𝑛 =𝑛! −1an=n!−1, log⁡(𝑛! −1) =𝑂(𝑛log⁡𝑛)log⁡(n!−1)=O(nlog⁡n) makes (𝑛! −1)1/𝜓𝑛 →1(n!−1)1/ψn→1 for every fixed 𝜓 >1ψ>1, so neither Erdős’s hypothesis lim sup𝑛𝑎1/2𝑛𝑛 =∞lim supnan1/2n=∞ nor the growth hypotheses of their Theorems 2 and 3 hold. These criteria do not decide 𝑆S; the useful content is the target these papers identify: a subsequence with clearing integers small enough for the corresponding remainders, or enough exact cancellation in those integers. Theorem 2.4 measures the cost of clearing all summands before reduction; it does not bound cancellation in their sum. Theorem 1.2 tests whether a maximal prime power survives reduction. Neither supplies the upper bound for a clearing integer, relative to its remainder, that these arguments need.

No irrationality conclusion is obtained here. The finite conclusion is that every rational representation 𝑆 =𝑎/𝑞S=a/q, 𝑞 >0q>0, must satisfy both 𝑞 ∤299999!q∤299999! and 𝑞 ≥239990 >1012038q≥239990>1012038. The criteria above require a condition at arbitrarily large indices. Extending either finite computation alone does not establish it.

Attribution. Wilson’s theorem and the Wilson reflection identity are classical, the latter recorded by Stewart [8]. The factorial-digit termination criterion goes back to Cantor [5]; Koepf and Schmersau prove its irrationality direction for digits that are not eventually maximal , and Galambos treats rationality criteria for Cantor series [6]. Here the identity 𝐶 =𝑆 −𝑒 +2C=S−e+2 gives the eventual digit value 𝑚 −2m−2 and extends to the shifted family. The comparison with Hančl and Tijdeman [11] concerns factorial scaling: their lemma makes a scaled tail integral, whereas the proof in §3 identifies the next integer above a generally nonintegral scaled prefix. The multiplicity bound is Garaev, Luca and Shparlinski’s , and the lcm deduction from it is not theirs. The divisibility in Lemma 2.2 is the case 𝑃 = −1P=−1 of the relation used in the proof of Lemma 5 of Luca and Shparlinski [13] and at display (2.5) of Lai . The nonvanishing cutoff for polynomial shifts is Lemma 3 of [13], restated with the bound 𝑛! +𝑃(𝑛) >1n!+P(n)>1 in [14]. The survival criterion is a specialisation of Louwsma and Martino’s valuation formula [4]. The single-denominator growth criterion is Erdős’s [3], and the continued-fraction identities are those of [17]. The deductions from Wilson’s theorem, the conditional finite support bound and Theorem 2.4 are proved above. No further priority claim is inferred from this comparison.

  • two indices sharing a prime power are farther apart than its exponent

  • the resulting bound on the number of such indices

  • the total relevant exponent is less than the prime

  • the total relevant exponent is less than the block diameter

  • a surviving prime has square greater than the parameter minus one

  • the projection moduli have the required lcm

  • the two-factor bound is no larger than the full residue bound

  • the valuation counts exponents occurring at two indices

  • a finite exponent range suffices for that count

  • the exact repeated-power criterion above the factorial base

Further deductions and limitations

This appendix supplies details used by the earlier sections: factorial digits and their remainders, exact gcd and lcm identities, and additional finite examples. It also records weaker deductions and explains why several proposed irrationality arguments do not establish their needed hypotheses.

For a real number 𝑥x, write 𝜃0 ={𝑥}θ0={x} and, for 𝑚 ≥1m≥1,

The converse holds for every real input, and gives Cantor’s termination criterion [5]

It does not show that the rational gaps admit a finite-state description or establish the unbounded non-unit carries needed for irrationality.

How the classical criteria apply here

Let 𝑠𝑛 <𝑎sn<a be partial sums tending to 𝑎a. Koepf and Schmersau show that ⌊𝑛𝑠𝑛⌋ =⌊𝑛𝑎⌋⌊nsn⌋=⌊na⌋ for all sufficiently large 𝑛n forces 𝑎a to be irrational [9]. A superseded deduction

A multiplicity theorem gives a weaker lcm bound, which is useful for comparison with the elementary proof in §2. For an odd prime 𝑟r, let 𝑚𝑟mr count the indices 2 ≤𝑛 ≤𝑁2≤n≤N with 𝑟 ∣𝑛! −1r∣n!−1; such an index satisfies 𝑛 <𝑟n<r. The factorial-congruence multiplicity estimate of Garaev, Luca and Shparlinski , applied to the residue 𝑎 =1a=1 on 1 ≤𝑛 ≤min(𝑁,𝑟 −1)1≤n≤min(N,r−1), gives 𝑚𝑟 ≪𝑁2/3mr≪N2/3; the prime 22 divides none of these factors. The sum of the exponents at a prime is at most the number of occurrences times the largest exponent, which is its exponent in 𝐿𝑁LN. Thus

𝑁∑𝑛=2log⁡(𝑛!−1)=∑𝑟𝑁∑𝑛=2𝑣𝑟(𝑛!−1)log⁡𝑟≤(max𝑟𝑚𝑟)log⁡𝐿𝑁≪𝑁2/3log⁡𝐿𝑁,∑n=2Nlog⁡(n!−1)=∑r∑n=2Nvr(n!−1)log⁡r≤(maxrmr)log⁡LN≪N2/3log⁡LN,

and Stirling’s formula makes the left side ≍𝑁2log⁡𝑁≍N2log⁡N, whence log⁡𝐿𝑁 ≫𝑁4/3log⁡𝑁log⁡LN≫N4/3log⁡N. Theorem 2.4 supersedes this: its exponent is 3/23/2, its constant is explicit, and it does not use the external multiplicity theorem. The deduction is retained because it is the only place a multiplicity bound enters the record.

Dividing all coefficients by their gcd does not evade the lcm restriction: the resulting integer vector still has 𝑉2 =⋯ =𝑉𝐷 =0V2=⋯=VD=0, so its moment is still divisible by 𝐿𝐷LD. For the nonzero cofactor vector in §7, normalization is justified by the elementary argument given there. It supplies no proof that the remainder is nonintegral. No formalised primitive cofactor construction is claimed here.

Rational grid points and first crossings

One can instead compare a partial sum 𝐻H with the rational numbers having a fixed positive denominator 𝑞q. The next such number above 𝐻H is (⌊𝑞𝐻⌋ +1)/𝑞(⌊qH⌋+1)/q. It is at most 𝑆S exactly when ⌊𝑞𝐻⌋ +1 ≤𝑞𝑆⌊qH⌋+1≤qS. Suppose 𝐻 <𝐺 ≤𝑆H<G≤S, the number 𝑛!𝐺n!G is an integer, and 𝑛!(𝑆 −𝐻) <1n!(S−H)<1. Then

The earlier record rejects a proposed divisibility strengthening of the first-crossing bound and reports examples at 𝑚 =52m=52 and 𝑚 =591m=591. Its notation for the rational quantity in that claim was not defined, so those reports are not used as a verified counterexample here. The established conclusion remains the lower bound on the denominator’s size, not a specified factor dividing it.

There is a second, more arithmetic mechanism at doubled prime indices, stated in long68:eq:doubled-prime. The formal theorem is not restricted to individually computed indices; the divisibility criterion holds for the actual partial sums at every odd prime.

The available squarefreeness evidence is finite. An exhaustive modular scan through 𝑟 ≤2,000,000r≤2,000,000 and 𝑛 ≤240n≤240 found four individual square hits and no prime with two such hits. All 498,501498,501 pairs 2 ≤𝑎 <𝑏 ≤10002≤a<b≤1000 have squarefree gcd(𝑎! −1,𝑏! −1)gcd(a!−1,b!−1). The supplied aggregate scan through 𝑝 =499p=499 also reports a ratio below 0.3740.374, but does not specify its logarithmic normalisation; that ratio is not used as a quantitative premise here. These are reported finite computations, not an asymptotic bound or a proof of squarefreeness at all indices.

A finite version of the argument for first prime occurrences compares the product of a chosen set of primes, each at least 55, with ∏2≤𝑘≤𝐵(𝑘! −1)∏2≤k≤B(k!−1); if the prime product is larger, at least one chosen prime has no hit through 𝐵B, while Wilson still bounds its least hit by 𝑞 −2q−2. Wilson reflection limits what a linear-size divisor can be assumed to be: if 𝑛n is odd, 𝑛 <𝑞n<q, and 𝑞 ∣𝑛! −1q∣n!−1, then 𝑞 ∣(𝑞 −𝑛 −1)! −1q∣(q−n−1)!−1. Suppose also that 𝑝 ≤𝑛p≤n, both indices lie in 𝐼𝑝Ip, and the reflected index is earlier, equivalently 𝑞 <2𝑛 +1q<2n+1. The prime 𝑞q then divides two denominators in the block. Since 𝑞 >𝑛 ≥𝑝q>n≥p, it does not divide 𝐹𝑝 =(𝑝 −1)!Fp=(p−1)!, so 𝑞 ∣˜𝐶𝑝q∣C~p: removing the factorial factor does not remove this shared prime.

Stewart states that for every 𝜀 >0ε>0 there are infinitely many odd 𝑛n whose least prime factor 𝑞q of 𝑛! −1n!−1 satisfies

𝑛<𝑞<(√145−18+𝜀)𝑛,n<q<(145−18+ε)n,

estimate (9) of Theorem 1 being stated for 𝑛! +1n!+1 [8] and transferred to 𝑛! −1n!−1 in the text [8]. This controls 𝑞q relative to the specified index 𝑛n, not to its first occurrence. It does not by itself force a repeated divisor. For the minus sign, the bound is already met at all sufficiently large Wilson indices 𝑛 =𝑞 −2n=q−2. For every prime 𝑞 ≥5q≥5, Wilson gives 𝑞 ∣(𝑞 −2)! −1q∣(q−2)!−1, and 𝑞q is its least prime factor. Indeed, every prime divisor exceeds 𝑞 −2q−2, and 𝑞 −1q−1 is even; moreover 𝑞/(𝑞 −2) →1q/(q−2)→1. The reflected index is then 11, outside the denominators of 𝑆S.

For example, modulo 1111 the only solution of 𝑘! ≡1k!≡1 with 2 ≤𝑘 ≤92≤k≤9 is 𝑘 =9k=9, although 11/9 <(√145 −1)/811/9<(145−1)/8. A small ratio 𝑞/𝑛q/n therefore supplies neither a second admissible hit nor membership of a reflected index in the chosen block. The earlier reflection argument needs both block-membership hypotheses and distinct indices. Neither the required estimate at first occurrences nor a bound for the total shared part follows from the transferred least-prime-factor estimate alone.

For a selected prime 𝑞 ∣𝑅𝑝q∣Rp, the factors 11 and 𝑞q are coprime, and the associated moduli 𝑅𝑝Rp and 𝑅𝑝/𝑞Rp/q have lcm 𝑅𝑝Rp. Thus this specialisation requires no second selected prime.

The elementary fact behind the projection argument is as follows. Let 𝑍,𝑇,𝐵Z,T,B be nonnegative integers, let 𝑅 >0R>0, and suppose 𝑍 ≡𝑇(mod𝑅)Z≡T(modR). Every positive divisor 𝑄Q of 𝑅R with 𝑍 ≤𝐵 <𝑄Z≤B<Q satisfies 𝑇mod𝑄 =𝑍TmodQ=Z, since 𝑍Z is already the least nonnegative representative. Consequently, unequal residues modulo two divisors exceeding 𝐵B rule out such a 𝑍Z. More generally, if 𝑇mod𝑄1 ≠𝑇mod𝑄2TmodQ1≠TmodQ2, then min(𝑄1,𝑄2) ≤𝑇min(Q1,Q2)≤T: otherwise both residues would equal 𝑇T.

Limits of the recurrences and clearing factors used here

  • Without the defining floor relation, the carry recurrence and its range allow 𝑍𝑚/𝑚!Zm/m! to be the constant 3/23/2. Taking 𝑍𝑚 =3𝑚!/2Zm=3m!/2 for 𝑚 ≥2m≥2 and 𝑏𝑚 =1bm=1 for 𝑚 ≥3m≥3 gives 𝑍𝑚 =𝑚𝑍𝑚−1 +1 −𝑏𝑚Zm=mZm−1+1−bm and −1 ≤𝑏𝑚 ≤𝑚 −1−1≤bm≤m−1, with the actual initial value 𝑍2 =3Z2=3. But it gives 𝑍3 =9Z3=9, whereas the actual prefix 𝐻3 =6/5H3=6/5 gives 𝑍3 =8Z3=8. This example only disproves sufficiency of the stated recurrence, bounds and initial integer. It fails the floor definition. No claim is made that it satisfies the additional prime-index identities. The rational recurrence for 𝐹𝑚 =𝑚!𝐻𝑚Fm=m!Hm in §B.1 determines the actual partial sums uniquely.

  • The arguments considered with Wilson quotients, harmonic sums, 𝑝p-adic gamma identities, and factorial residues still need a real gap estimate and the required modular divisibility at the same indices. No such unbounded family is obtained here. This records the missing step in these arguments, not an impossibility theorem for the use of those identities.

  • For the genus-zero product 𝐸(𝑧) =∏𝑛≥2(1 −𝑧/𝑛!)E(z)=∏n≥2(1−z/n!), local uniform convergence and logarithmic differentiation give −𝐸′(1)/𝐸(1) =𝑆−E′(1)/E(1)=S. Termwise clearing by ∏𝑁𝑛=2(𝑛! −1)∏n=2N(n!−1) cannot give a positive remainder tending to zero: this product is at least 𝐿𝑁LN, and 𝐿𝑁(𝑆 −𝐻𝑁) →∞LN(S−HN)→∞ by §2. The conclusion concerns this clearing factor alone; Hermite–Padé systems with other denominators are not ruled out.

  • Changing a coefficient vector without changing its moment changes the residual by an integer only. Also, cancelling the first 𝐷 −1D−1 weighted sums forces 𝐿𝐷LD to divide the moment; factorial divisibility does not remove that constraint.

  • A fixed pair of denominator indices cannot make the projection argument work at arbitrarily large parameters, because their factors eventually divide the factorial being removed.

An elementary criterion for any real number

The fractional-part condition in (10) follows from the following consequence of Cantor’s termination criterion. For a real 𝑥x and any positive sequence 𝑐𝑚cm with 𝑐𝑚 ≤1/𝑚cm≤1/m eventually,

𝑥∉ℚ⟺{(𝑚−1)!𝑥}≥𝑐𝑚 for arbitrarily large 𝑚.x∉Q⟺{(m−1)!x}≥cm for arbitrarily large m.

For rational 𝑥x the fractional parts vanish eventually. Conversely, if {(𝑚 −1)!𝑥} <𝑐𝑚 ≤1/𝑚{(m−1)!x}<cm≤1/m for all large 𝑚m, then 𝑚{(𝑚 −1)!𝑥} <1m{(m−1)!x}<1, so every sufficiently late canonical digit is zero. Cantor’s criterion then makes 𝑥x rational. Equality 𝑐𝑚 =1/𝑚cm=1/m is allowed: it is failure of the displayed weak inequality that makes 𝑚{(𝑚 −1)!𝑥}m{(m−1)!x} strictly less than one. For 𝑥 =𝑆x=S, the choice 𝑐𝑚 =𝐸𝑚/𝑚cm=Em/m gives exactly (10); indeed 0 <𝐸𝑚 <10<Em<1 ensures the required threshold bound. The finite test long68:eq:finite-escape is a separate sufficient condition at one index. Its cofinal converse uses the carry theorem, as shown in §3, not substitution into this general criterion. Neither argument proves that 𝑆S meets the test at arbitrarily large indices.

The threshold 1/𝑚1/m cannot be replaced by 𝜆/𝑚λ/m for a fixed 𝜆 >1λ>1. For 𝑥 =𝑒x=e and 𝑚 ≥3m≥3, the factorial tail gives

𝑚{(𝑚−1)!𝑒}=1+𝑚!∑𝑛>𝑚1𝑛!<1+1𝑚<𝜆eventually.m{(m−1)!e}=1+m!∑n>m1n!<1+1m<λeventually.

Thus the irrational number 𝑒e would never meet the enlarged threshold at sufficiently large indices. Positivity is also essential: with 𝑐𝑚 =0cm=0, rational numbers would meet the threshold eventually. These examples explain the two assumptions without imposing any equidistribution hypothesis.

Relations among the criteria

The two finite exclusions in §6 use only the carry criterion and a rational enclosure. The coefficient constructions do not enter either calculation. They instead produce integer linear forms R(𝑐) =𝑀(𝑐)𝑆 +𝑘R(c)=M(c)S+k, 𝑘 ∈ℤk∈Z. At fixed moment, changing coefficients changes only 𝑘k; primitive cofactors on the stated progression reproduce the explicit progression vector rather than a new family.

For a rational value 𝑆 =𝑎/𝑞S=a/q, such a form is integral whenever 𝑞 ∣𝑀(𝑐)q∣M(c). To extend this method beyond finite exclusions, one therefore needs nonintegral remainders with moments covering every positive denominator in this divisibility sense. The common-denominator lower bound and the prime-power survival test do not supply the needed upper bound for a remainder relative to its integer gap. Likewise, the equivalent carry, digit and interval criteria still require events at arbitrarily large indices. A finite calculation can rule out denominators without proving any of those unbounded assertions.
